intro: At B1 you learnt how to write a polite email. Now let's look at the words inside it: English has many pairs like ask and enquire, or find out and discover, with the same meaning but a different level of formality. You'll learn the formal partners of common words and phrasal verbs, and how to choose the right one for a job application, a client or a colleague on WhatsApp.
teachingNotes: Build on b1-emails (Dear Mr / Ms + surname, Dear Pak Budi with Indonesian colleagues, Could you …?, I'm writing to ask about …, Best regards / Kind regards, no emoji or chat forms in semi-formal emails), b1-phrasal-verbs (set up, put off, call off, look into, find out, turn down …) and b2-phrasal-verbs-idioms (separable / three-part phrasal verbs, idioms like break the ice). Recap in a line, don't re-teach. New here: the WORDS change with the register (tingkat formalitas). The core message: informal words and phrasal verbs are NOT wrong, just less formal; formal words in a chat sound stiff. Never mark a correct informal word as an error: say it's correct but less formal for this reader, and ask which word is MORE formal or better for this reader. At B2 register is a tendency, not a law: real emails mix levels a little.

Formal equivalents (objective formal-equivalents): get → receive (an email, a payment, a letter) / obtain (a visa, permission, a certificate: with effort); ask about → enquire about (British) / inquire about (American), ask for → request (not 'enquire a refund'); help → assist (assist you with …); need → require (rules and conditions; 'I require a coffee' sounds funny); buy → purchase (also a noun); start → begin → commence (very formal: ceremonies, invitations, contracts; in normal emails prefer start / begin); tell → inform (inform you that … / inform us of …: the Indonesian trap 'inform to you' from 'menginformasikan kepada Anda'; same with 'assist to you'); enough → sufficient (+ noun, or after be; 'big enough' never becomes 'big sufficient'); about → regarding / concerning (only 'about a topic', never 'approximately': 'regarding 30 people' ✗).

Phrasal vs Latin-based verbs (objective phrasal-vs-latin): find out → discover / learn, put off → postpone, call off → cancel, look into → investigate, go up / go down → increase / decrease, set up → establish (a company) but set up a meeting → arrange, come back → return, talk about → discuss, turn down → decline. Latin-based = one word from Latin, often via French, many look like Indonesian loanwords (investigasi, diskusi, informasi). Traps: the formal verb takes no particle ('discuss about' ✗ from berdiskusi tentang, 'return back' ✗, 'postpone off' ✗, 'investigate into' ✗); postpone (diundur) ≠ cancel (batal); some phrasal verbs stay even in formal writing (I look forward to hearing from you).

Matching the reader (objective match-the-reader) and the node's common errors: 'Hi Sir, I wanna ask about the job.' → 'Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to enquire about the position.' (Hi + Sir don't mix; Sir + first name = a British knight's title; wanna / gonna are spoken or chat forms, never in an email; 'Yes, sir' to a customer in speech is fine). 'Dear Mr Budi' when Budi is the first name → 'Dear Mr Santoso' (Mr / Ms + surname). Many Indonesians have one name (Wahyudi) → 'Dear Mr Wahyudi' is right; if unsure which part is the family name → full name ('Dear Budi Santoso,'); with Indonesian colleagues in Indonesia, 'Dear Pak Budi,' / 'Dear Bu Ani,' is the normal local custom. 'Thanks a lot, see ya!' → 'Thank you for your help. Kind regards,'. Three model readers: job application / bank / official letter (formal), email to a client (semi-formal), WhatsApp to a colleague (informal).

Limits: grammar is A0–B1 plus the chain. No passive beyond present / past simple (say 'We have postponed the meeting', not 'The meeting has been postponed'); no 'Please find attached' (teach 'I've attached …'); no inversion ('Should you require …'), no participle clauses. Don't teach rare stiff words (ascertain, endeavour, hereby, henceforth, utilise): if the learner uses one correctly, accept it and say it's very formal. Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully only as information (very formal British letters), never tested. Contexts: job applications, banks, hotels, clients, Jakarta offices, WhatsApp with colleagues. Correct one thing at a time, usually Mr + first name, 'inform to you', 'discuss about', or a word that's too formal or too informal for the reader.

keyPoints.title: Formal partners of everyday words
keyPoints.explanation: In formal writing, swap everyday words for their formal partners: get → receive (an email, a payment) or obtain (a visa, permission), ask about → enquire about (British) / inquire about (American), ask for → request, help → assist, need → require, buy → purchase, start → begin / commence (very formal), tell → inform, enough → sufficient, about → regarding / concerning. Choose by meaning, and watch the grammar: inform you that … and assist you with … (not 'inform to you').

examples.en: I am writing to enquire about your evening courses.
examples.id: Saya menulis untuk menanyakan kursus malam Anda.

examples.en: You must obtain a visa before you travel.
examples.id: Anda harus memperoleh visa sebelum bepergian.

examples.en: Please inform us if you require any assistance.
examples.id: Mohon beri tahu kami jika Anda memerlukan bantuan.

id.title: Padanan formal untuk kata sehari-hari
id.explanation: Dalam tulisan formal, ganti kata sehari-hari dengan padanan formalnya: get → receive (menerima email, pembayaran) atau obtain (memperoleh visa, izin), ask about → enquire about (British) / inquire about (American), ask for → request, help → assist, need → require, buy → purchase, start → begin / commence (sangat formal), tell → inform, enough → sufficient, about → regarding / concerning. Pilih berdasarkan arti, dan perhatikan tata bahasanya: inform you that … dan assist you with … (bukan 'inform to you').

keyPoints.title: Phrasal verb or Latin-based verb?
keyPoints.explanation: Phrasal verbs (find out, put off, look into, go up, set up) are everyday English and never wrong. In reports, official letters and job applications, a one-word Latin-based verb sounds more formal: discover, postpone, investigate, increase, establish (also call off → cancel, come back → return, talk about → discuss, turn down → decline). The formal verb has no small word: discuss the plan, not 'discuss about the plan'. Choose by meaning: set up a company → establish, but set up a meeting → arrange.

examples.en: The auditors discovered several errors in the report.
examples.id: Para auditor menemukan beberapa kesalahan di laporan itu.

examples.en: The number of complaints decreased last month.
We need to discuss the new budget.

id.title: Phrasal verb atau kata kerja dari bahasa Latin?
id.explanation: Phrasal verb (find out, put off, look into, go up, set up) adalah bahasa Inggris sehari-hari dan tidak pernah salah. Di laporan, surat resmi dan lamaran kerja, kata kerja satu kata dari bahasa Latin terdengar lebih formal: discover, postpone, investigate, increase, establish (juga call off → cancel, come back → return, talk about → discuss, turn down → decline). Kata kerja formalnya tidak memakai kata kecil: discuss the plan, bukan 'discuss about the plan'. Pilih berdasarkan arti: set up a company → establish, tapi set up a meeting → arrange.

keyPoints.title: Match the reader
keyPoints.explanation: Ask who is reading. A job application, a bank or an official letter → formal: Dear Ms Tan, / Dear Sir or Madam, full forms, formal verbs, no idioms, Kind regards. An email to a client → semi-formal: polite and clear, some formal words, common phrasal verbs are fine, Best regards. A WhatsApp to a colleague → informal: Hi Dimas!, contractions, phrasal verbs, Thanks!. Names: Mr / Ms + surname (Dear Mr Santoso, not Dear Mr Budi); a one-name Indonesian → that name (Dear Mr Wahyudi); not sure → the full name; Indonesian colleagues in Indonesia → Dear Pak Budi, / Dear Bu Ani,. Never 'Hi Sir', never 'wanna' or 'see ya' in an email.

examples.en: Thank you for your help. Kind regards,
examples.id: Terima kasih atas bantuan Anda. Salam,

examples.en: Thanks a lot, see you tomorrow!

id.title: Sesuaikan dengan pembaca
id.explanation: Tanyakan siapa yang membaca. Lamaran kerja, bank atau surat resmi → formal: Dear Ms Tan, / Dear Sir or Madam, bentuk lengkap, kata kerja formal, tanpa idiom, Kind regards. Email ke klien → semi-formal: sopan dan jelas, beberapa kata formal, phrasal verb yang umum tidak masalah, Best regards. WhatsApp ke rekan kerja → informal: Hi Dimas!, kontraksi, phrasal verb, Thanks!. Nama: Mr / Ms + nama keluarga (Dear Mr Santoso, bukan Dear Mr Budi); orang Indonesia dengan satu nama → nama itu (Dear Mr Wahyudi); tidak yakin → nama lengkap; rekan kerja Indonesia di Indonesia → Dear Pak Budi, / Dear Bu Ani,. Jangan pernah 'Hi Sir', jangan 'wanna' atau 'see ya' di email.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write one formal verb that means needs: 'The position ___ at least two years of experience in sales.'
guidedPractice.hint: need → require, a formal verb for rules and conditions. The subject is the position (it), so add -s: requires.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write one formal word that means about (a topic): 'I am writing ___ the invoice you sent on 12 June.'
guidedPractice.hint: about (= tentang) → regarding or concerning. Not 'regarding' for 'sekitar': that's approximately.

guidedPractice.prompt: Replace turned down with one formal verb in the past simple: 'Sari turned down the job offer from the Surabaya office.'
guidedPractice.hint: turn down an offer or an invitation (menolak) → decline. Past simple: declined.

guidedPractice.prompt: You're messaging your futsal friends on WhatsApp. Which verb fits better, postpone or put off? 'Shall we ___ the match till next week? It's raining.'
guidedPractice.hint: A WhatsApp to friends is informal, so the phrasal verb put off fits better. postpone is correct too, but it sounds like an official notice.

independentPractice.prompt: Correct the mistake: The team will discuss about the new office rules on Monday.
expected: the team will discuss the new office rules on monday
independentPractice.hint: discuss already means talk about, so no about after it (from berdiskusi tentang).

independentPractice.prompt: Rewrite for an email to a client (no chat forms): I wanna know the price.
expected: i would like to know the price
i'd like to know the price
i would like to enquire about the price
i would like to inquire about the price
independentPractice.hint: wanna is spoken English and chat spelling. In an email: I would like to …

independentPractice.prompt: Write the formal verb for bought (past simple): 'I ___ two tickets on your website, but I did not receive a confirmation email.'

assessment.prompt: Complete this formal reply to a client with one formal verb that means got (past simple): 'Dear Mr Lim, Thank you for your email. We ___ your payment of Rp 4,500,000 yesterday, and your order will arrive on Friday.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: received (get a payment, an email or a letter → receive). 'have received' = 60 (the right verb, but yesterday needs the past simple). 'got' = 30 (right meaning, but the task asks for the formal verb). 'obtained' = 20 (obtain is for something you get with effort, like a visa or permission, not a payment someone sends you). 'receive' = 70 (right verb, wrong form).

assessment.prompt: Complete this message from a bank with one formal word that means enough: 'We are sorry, but there are not ___ funds in your account to complete this transfer.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: sufficient (enough → sufficient, before a noun). 'adequate' = 100. 'enough' = 30 (correct English, but the task asks for the formal word). 'sufficiently' = 40 (wrong form: an adverb can't go before the noun funds).

assessment.prompt: Complete this line from a hotel's website with one formal verb that means help: 'Our staff will be happy to ___ you with any questions about your booking.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: assist (help → assist; assist + the person + with). 'help' = 30 (right meaning, but not the formal word). 'support' = 50 (formal, but it means giving support over time, not answering questions). 'assist to' = 40 (assist takes the person directly).

assessment.prompt: Make this sentence from a company report more formal: replace the phrasal verb with one Latin-based verb in the same form. 'The IT department is looking into the problem with the payroll system.' Write only the new verb.
assessment.rubric: Correct: investigating (look into → investigate, -ing form after is). 'examining' = 100. 'investigate' = 60 (right verb, wrong form). 'investigating into' = 50 (the formal verb takes no small word). 'addressing' or 'reviewing' = 70 (formal, but a slightly different meaning: dealing with or checking, not finding the cause). 'checking' = 40 (right meaning, but not more formal).

assessment.prompt: Replace went up with one formal verb in the past simple, for a company report: 'In 2025, the price of cooking oil in Surabaya went up by 15%.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: increased (go up → increase, past simple). 'rose' = 100 (also normal in reports). 'climbed' = 80. 'increase' = 60 (wrong form). 'raised' = 30 (raise needs an object: the shops raised the price). 'decreased' = 0 (opposite meaning).

assessment.prompt: You're writing a formal email to a buyer at a company in Singapore. His name is Andi Wijaya, and Wijaya is his surname (family name). Write the greeting (a comma is optional).
assessment.rubric: Correct: Dear Mr Wijaya (Mr + surname; 'Mr.' with a full stop is the American spelling, also fine). 'Dear Mr Andi Wijaya' or 'Dear Andi Wijaya' = 70 (polite, but here you know the surname, so Mr + surname is the standard). 'Dear Pak Andi' = 50 (the Indonesian custom, fine with colleagues in Indonesia, less suitable for a formal international email). 'Dear Mr Andi' = 0 (Mr + first name: the classic mistake). 'Hi Sir' or 'Dear Sir' = 0. A comma after the greeting is optional; assess the greeting, not the comma.

assessment.prompt: You're sending a WhatsApp message to Dimas, a colleague who sits near you. Which message fits this reader better? Write A or B. A: 'Could you inform me once the client arrives? Kind regards, Rina' B: 'Can you let me know when the client gets here? Thanks!'
assessment.rubric: Correct: B (a WhatsApp to a colleague is informal: let me know, gets here, Thanks!). A = 0: its English is correct, but inform, once and Kind regards are for a formal email and sound stiff in a chat.

material.title: Register: the same message for different readers

id.title: Register: pesan yang sama untuk pembaca yang berbeda

blocks.text:
Quick recap from B1: a semi-formal email starts with *Dear Mr / Ms + surname,*, asks politely with *Could you …?* and ends with *Best regards,*. At B2 the **words themselves** change too.

**Register** (how formal your English sounds) works like Indonesian: *nanya* in a chat, *bertanya* in normal speech, *menanyakan* or *memohon informasi* in a letter. English has three rough levels:
- **Informal**: friends, family, colleagues you know well, WhatsApp. Phrasal verbs, **contractions** (short forms: *I'm, can't, we've*), *Thanks!*
- **Neutral / semi-formal**: most work emails, a client you know. Clear and polite: everyday words with a few formal ones.
- **Formal**: a job application, a bank, a university, an official letter, a reader you don't know. Formal one-word verbs, full forms (*I am, we would*), no idioms.

These are **tendencies, not strict rules**: real emails often mix the levels a little. The skill is choosing for **your reader**.

id.text:
Ulasan singkat dari B1: email semi-formal dimulai dengan *Dear Mr / Ms + nama keluarga,*, meminta dengan sopan memakai *Could you …?* dan ditutup dengan *Best regards,*. Di B2, **kata-katanya sendiri** juga berubah.

**Register** (tingkat formalitas bahasa Inggrismu) mirip dengan bahasa Indonesia: *nanya* di chat, *bertanya* dalam obrolan biasa, *menanyakan* atau *memohon informasi* di surat. Bahasa Inggris punya kira-kira tiga tingkat:
- **Informal**: teman, keluarga, rekan kerja yang sudah akrab, WhatsApp. Phrasal verb, **kontraksi** (bentuk singkat: *I'm, can't, we've*), *Thanks!*
- **Netral / semi-formal**: kebanyakan email kerja, klien yang sudah kamu kenal. Jelas dan sopan: kata sehari-hari dengan beberapa kata formal.
- **Formal**: lamaran kerja, bank, universitas, surat resmi, pembaca yang tidak kamu kenal. Kata kerja formal satu kata, bentuk lengkap (*I am, we would*), tanpa idiom.

Ini **kecenderungan, bukan aturan kaku**: email sungguhan sering sedikit mencampur tingkatnya. Kuncinya adalah memilih sesuai **pembacamu**.

rows.en: Can you tell me if you need any help?
rows.id: Bisa kasih tahu aku kalau kamu butuh bantuan?
rows.note: informal: a chat with a colleague

rows.en: Please let me know if you need any help.
rows.id: Tolong beri tahu saya kalau Anda butuh bantuan.
rows.note: neutral: a normal work email

rows.en: Please inform us if you require any assistance.
rows.id: Mohon beri tahu kami jika Anda memerlukan bantuan.
rows.note: formal: a letter from a bank or a hotel

id.note: formal: surat dari bank atau hotel

blocks.text: **Informal is not wrong.** *find out, ask, buy, tell* are perfectly correct English: they're just the everyday choice. And formal words in the wrong place sound strange: *I will purchase the snacks* in a WhatsApp to a friend sounds like a robot (or a joke). Formal doesn't mean long and complicated either: a short, clear sentence with the right words is the goal. Idioms like *break the ice* (from the last lesson) are informal too: great in conversation, but leave them out of a formal letter.

id.text: **Informal itu tidak salah.** *find out, ask, buy, tell* adalah bahasa Inggris yang benar: hanya saja itu pilihan sehari-hari. Dan kata formal di tempat yang salah terdengar aneh: *I will purchase the snacks* di WhatsApp ke teman terdengar seperti robot (atau bercanda). Formal juga bukan berarti panjang dan rumit: tujuannya kalimat pendek dan jelas dengan kata yang tepat. Idiom seperti *break the ice* (dari pelajaran sebelumnya) juga informal: bagus untuk percakapan, tapi jangan dipakai di surat formal.

blocks.prompt: Your friend Sari asks in your WhatsApp group who's bringing snacks to the party. Which reply fits best?
options: I will purchase the snacks for the party.
I'll buy the snacks for the party!
I shall obtain the snacks for the party.
blocks.explain: A WhatsApp to a friend is informal, so the everyday verb **buy** and the contraction *I'll* fit. *purchase* and *obtain* are correct English, but they belong in formal writing: here they sound stiff, like a robot.

id.prompt: Temanmu Sari bertanya di grup WhatsApp siapa yang membawa camilan ke pesta. Balasan mana yang paling cocok?
id.explain: WhatsApp ke teman itu informal, jadi kata kerja sehari-hari **buy** dan kontraksi *I'll* yang cocok. *purchase* dan *obtain* itu bahasa Inggris yang benar, tapi tempatnya di tulisan formal: di sini terdengar kaku, seperti robot.

material.title: Everyday words and their formal partners

blocks.text:
In formal writing, many everyday words have a **formal partner** with the same meaning. Learn them in pairs:
- **get** → **receive** (an email, a letter, a payment) or **obtain** (a visa, permission, a certificate: something you get with some effort)
- **ask about** → **enquire about** (British) / **inquire about** (American); **ask for** → **request**
- **help** → **assist** (*assist you **with** your application*)
- **need** → **require** (mostly rules and conditions: *This visa requires a letter from your employer.*)
- **buy** → **purchase** (also a noun: *Thank you for your purchase.*)
- **start** → **begin** (neutral) → **commence** (very formal)
- **tell** → **inform** (*inform you **that** …*, *inform us **of** any changes*)
- **enough** → **sufficient** (+ a noun: *sufficient time*)
- **about** → **regarding** / **concerning** (*Regarding your question, …*)

id.text:
Dalam tulisan formal, banyak kata sehari-hari punya **padanan formal** dengan arti yang sama. Hafalkan berpasangan:
- **get** → **receive** (menerima email, surat, pembayaran) atau **obtain** (memperoleh visa, izin, sertifikat: sesuatu yang kamu dapat dengan usaha)
- **ask about** → **enquire about** (British) / **inquire about** (American) = menanyakan; **ask for** → **request** = meminta
- **help** → **assist** = membantu (*assist you **with** your application*)
- **need** → **require** = memerlukan (biasanya untuk aturan dan syarat: *This visa requires a letter from your employer.*)
- **buy** → **purchase** = membeli (juga kata benda: *Thank you for your purchase.* = Terima kasih atas pembelian Anda.)
- **start** → **begin** (netral) → **commence** (sangat formal) = mulai
- **tell** → **inform** = memberitahukan (*inform you **that** …*, *inform us **of** any changes*)
- **enough** → **sufficient** = cukup (+ kata benda: *sufficient time*)
- **about** → **regarding** / **concerning** = mengenai, tentang (*Regarding your question, …*)

rows.en: I received your letter this morning.
rows.id: Saya menerima surat Anda tadi pagi.
rows.note: get a letter → receive

rows.en: You must obtain a visa before you travel.
rows.id: Anda harus memperoleh visa sebelum bepergian.
rows.note: get a visa (with some effort) → obtain

rows.en: I am writing to enquire about your evening courses.
rows.id: Saya menulis untuk menanyakan kursus malam Anda.
rows.note: ask about → enquire about (American: inquire about)

id.note: ask about → enquire about (American: inquire about)

rows.en: I would like to request a refund.
rows.id: Saya ingin meminta pengembalian dana.
rows.note: ask for → request

rows.en: The ceremony will commence at 9 a.m.
rows.id: Upacaranya akan dimulai pukul 9 pagi.
rows.note: very formal: official events, invitations, contracts

id.note: sangat formal: acara resmi, undangan, kontrak

rows.en: Regarding your question, the office opens at 8.
rows.id: Mengenai pertanyaan Anda, kantornya buka pukul 8.
rows.note: regarding = about a topic

blocks.text:
**Traps.**
1) **inform** and **assist** take the person directly: *We would like to inform **you** that …*, not *inform to you* ✗ (from *menginformasikan kepada Anda*). Same with *assist you*, not *assist to you* ✗.
2) Choose by **meaning**. *get* has many meanings: *I got your email* → *I **received** your email*, but *I got a visa* → *I **obtained** a visa*. And *get tired* (= become) has neither partner.
3) *enquire about* asks for **information**. To ask for a thing, use **request**: *request a refund*, not *enquire a refund* ✗.
4) **regarding** means *tentang*, never *sekitar*: *about 30 people* → *approximately 30 people*, not *regarding 30 people* ✗.
5) **sufficient** goes before a noun or after *be*: *sufficient time*, *The time is sufficient.* But *big enough* stays *big enough* (not *big sufficient* ✗).
6) **commence** is very formal: in most work emails, *start* or *begin* sounds better.

id.text:
**Jebakan.**
1) **inform** dan **assist** langsung diikuti orangnya: *We would like to inform **you** that …*, bukan *inform to you* ✗ (dari *menginformasikan kepada Anda*). Sama dengan *assist you*, bukan *assist to you* ✗.
2) Pilih berdasarkan **arti**. *get* punya banyak arti: *I got your email* → *I **received** your email*, tapi *I got a visa* → *I **obtained** a visa*. Dan *get tired* (= menjadi lelah) tidak punya padanan dari daftar ini.
3) *enquire about* untuk menanyakan **informasi**. Untuk meminta sesuatu, pakai **request**: *request a refund*, bukan *enquire a refund* ✗.
4) **regarding** artinya *tentang*, bukan *sekitar*: *about 30 people* (sekitar 30 orang) → *approximately 30 people*, bukan *regarding 30 people* ✗.
5) **sufficient** dipakai sebelum kata benda atau setelah *be*: *sufficient time*, *The time is sufficient.* Tapi *big enough* tetap *big enough* (bukan *big sufficient* ✗).
6) **commence** sangat formal: di kebanyakan email kerja, *start* atau *begin* terdengar lebih pas.

options: The meeting will start regarding 10 a.m.
Regarding your question about parking, there is a car park behind the office.
There were regarding 30 people at the meeting.
blocks.explain: **regarding** means 'about a topic' (*tentang, mengenai*), so it fits *Regarding your question …*. It never means 'approximately' (*sekitar*): for times and numbers, say *about 10 a.m.* or *approximately 30 people*.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang memakai regarding dengan benar?
id.explain: **regarding** artinya 'tentang suatu topik' (*tentang, mengenai*), jadi cocok di *Regarding your question …*. Kata ini tidak pernah berarti *sekitar*: untuk jam dan angka, pakai *about 10 a.m.* atau *approximately 30 people*.

material.title: Phrasal verb or one formal verb?

id.title: Phrasal verb atau satu kata kerja formal?

blocks.text:
In B1 and in the last lesson you learnt many **phrasal verbs** (a verb + a small word with a new meaning: *look into, put off*). They're everyday English: natural in speech, chats and friendly emails. Most of them have a **one-word partner** that sounds more formal. These are often called **Latin-based verbs**: they come from Latin (often through French), and many look like Indonesian loanwords: *investigate* (investigasi), *discuss* (diskusi), *inform* (informasi).
- **find out** → **discover** (or *learn*)
- **put off** → **postpone** (it still happens, later)
- **call off** → **cancel** (it doesn't happen)
- **look into** → **investigate** (a problem, a complaint)
- **go up / go down** → **increase / decrease** (prices, numbers)
- **set up** → **establish** (a company, an organisation)
- **come back** → **return**
- **talk about** → **discuss**
- **turn down** → **decline** (an offer, an invitation)

A phrasal verb is **never wrong** just because it's informal. In a meeting, a native speaker says *Let's look into it.* In a written report, *We will investigate the problem.* sounds more professional.

id.text:
Di B1 dan di pelajaran sebelumnya kamu sudah belajar banyak **phrasal verb** (kata kerja + kata kecil dengan arti baru: *look into, put off*). Itu bahasa Inggris sehari-hari: wajar dalam percakapan, chat dan email santai. Kebanyakan punya **pasangan satu kata** yang terdengar lebih formal. Ini sering disebut **kata kerja dari bahasa Latin** (Latin-based verbs): asalnya dari bahasa Latin (sering lewat bahasa Prancis), dan banyak yang mirip kata serapan bahasa Indonesia: *investigate* (investigasi), *discuss* (diskusi), *inform* (informasi).
- **find out** → **discover** (atau *learn*) = mengetahui, menemukan
- **put off** → **postpone** = menunda (acaranya tetap ada, nanti)
- **call off** → **cancel** = membatalkan (acaranya tidak jadi)
- **look into** → **investigate** = menyelidiki, memeriksa (masalah, keluhan)
- **go up / go down** → **increase / decrease** = naik / turun (harga, angka)
- **set up** → **establish** = mendirikan (perusahaan, organisasi)
- **come back** → **return** = kembali
- **talk about** → **discuss** = membahas, mendiskusikan
- **turn down** → **decline** = menolak (tawaran, undangan)

Phrasal verb **tidak pernah salah** hanya karena informal. Dalam rapat, penutur asli bilang *Let's look into it.* Di laporan tertulis, *We will investigate the problem.* terdengar lebih profesional.

rows.en: The auditors discovered several errors in the report.

rows.note: formal: a report (find out → discover)

rows.en: Sorry, we have to put off dinner till next week.
rows.id: Maaf, kita harus menunda makan malamnya sampai minggu depan.
rows.note: informal: a message to a friend

rows.en: The company has decided to cancel the event because of the flood.
rows.id: Perusahaan memutuskan untuk membatalkan acara itu karena banjir.
rows.note: formal: an announcement (call off → cancel)

rows.en: The number of complaints decreased last month.
rows.id: Jumlah keluhan turun bulan lalu.
rows.note: formal: a report (go down → decrease)

rows.en: We need to discuss the new budget.

rows.note: talk about → discuss (no about after discuss)

id.note: talk about → discuss (tanpa about setelah discuss)

blocks.text:
**Traps.**
1) The formal verb **doesn't take the small word**: *discuss about* ✗ (from *berdiskusi tentang*), *return back* ✗, *postpone off* ✗. Say *discuss the plan*, *return to Jakarta*, *postpone the meeting*.
2) Choose by **meaning**: one phrasal verb can have several meanings. *set up a company* → **establish**, but *set up a meeting* → **arrange**.
3) *put off* ≠ *call off*: **postpone** = it happens later (*diundur*), **cancel** = it doesn't happen (*batal*).
4) Don't swap every phrasal verb. Some are fine even in formal writing: *I look forward to hearing from you* is the normal formal closing line.

id.text:
**Jebakan.**
1) Kata kerja formalnya **tidak memakai kata kecil**: *discuss about* ✗ (dari *berdiskusi tentang*), *return back* ✗, *postpone off* ✗. Yang benar *discuss the plan*, *return to Jakarta*, *postpone the meeting*.
2) Pilih berdasarkan **arti**: satu phrasal verb bisa punya beberapa arti. *set up a company* (mendirikan perusahaan) → **establish**, tapi *set up a meeting* (mengatur rapat) → **arrange**.
3) *put off* ≠ *call off*: **postpone** = acaranya tetap ada nanti (*diundur*), **cancel** = acaranya tidak jadi (*batal*).
4) Jangan ganti semua phrasal verb. Ada yang tetap pas di tulisan formal: *I look forward to hearing from you* adalah kalimat penutup formal yang biasa.

blocks.prompt: Which formal verb can replace set up here? 'Could you set up a meeting with the client for Thursday?'
blocks.explain: Here *set up* means organising a meeting (*mengatur*), so the formal partner is **arrange**. *establish* is for a company or an organisation (*mendirikan*), and *install* is for software or a machine.

id.prompt: Kata kerja formal mana yang bisa menggantikan set up di sini? 'Could you set up a meeting with the client for Thursday?'
id.explain: Di sini *set up* artinya mengatur rapat, jadi padanan formalnya **arrange**. *establish* untuk perusahaan atau organisasi (*mendirikan*), dan *install* untuk software atau mesin (*memasang*).

material.title: Match the reader: names, greetings and endings

id.title: Sesuaikan dengan pembaca: nama, salam dan penutup

blocks.text:
Before you write, ask: **who is reading, and how well do I know them?**
- **A job application, a bank, a university, an official letter** → formal. *Dear Ms Tan,* or, with no name, *Dear Sir or Madam,*. Full forms (*I am writing to …*), formal verbs (*enquire, require, assist*), no idioms. End with *Kind regards,*. Very formal British letters end *Yours sincerely,* (after *Dear Ms Tan,*) or *Yours faithfully,* (after *Dear Sir or Madam,*); American English uses *Sincerely,*.
- **An email to a client** → semi-formal. *Dear Mr Lim,*, polite requests, some formal words (*regarding, inform*); common phrasal verbs are fine, and so is *I'm* with a client you know. End with *Best regards,*.
- **A WhatsApp to a colleague** → informal. *Hi Dimas!* (or *Pak Hasan,* for an older Indonesian colleague), contractions, phrasal verbs, *Thanks!*. No *Dear*, no *Kind regards*.

**Names.** In English it's **Mr / Ms + surname** (the family name). Budi Santoso, if Santoso is his family name → *Dear Mr Santoso,*, not *Dear Mr Budi* ✗: Mr + a first name is neither the English custom nor the Indonesian one. Many Indonesians have **only one name** (*Wahyudi*): then that is the whole name, so *Dear Mr Wahyudi,* is right. If you aren't sure which part is the family name, write the **full name**: *Dear Budi Santoso,*. With Indonesian colleagues in Indonesia, *Dear Pak Budi,* / *Dear Bu Ani,* is normal and polite: that's the local custom (Pak / Bu + the name people call them).

id.text:
Sebelum menulis, tanyakan: **siapa yang membaca, dan seberapa kenal aku dengannya?**
- **Lamaran kerja, bank, universitas, surat resmi** → formal. *Dear Ms Tan,* atau, kalau tidak tahu namanya, *Dear Sir or Madam,*. Bentuk lengkap (*I am writing to …*), kata kerja formal (*enquire, require, assist*), tanpa idiom. Tutup dengan *Kind regards,*. Surat British yang sangat formal ditutup dengan *Yours sincerely,* (setelah *Dear Ms Tan,*) atau *Yours faithfully,* (setelah *Dear Sir or Madam,*); bahasa Inggris Amerika memakai *Sincerely,*.
- **Email ke klien** → semi-formal. *Dear Mr Lim,*, permintaan yang sopan, beberapa kata formal (*regarding, inform*); phrasal verb yang umum tidak masalah, begitu juga *I'm* dengan klien yang sudah kamu kenal. Tutup dengan *Best regards,*.
- **WhatsApp ke rekan kerja** → informal. *Hi Dimas!* (atau *Pak Hasan,* untuk rekan kerja Indonesia yang lebih senior), kontraksi, phrasal verb, *Thanks!*. Tanpa *Dear*, tanpa *Kind regards*.

**Nama.** Dalam bahasa Inggris aturannya **Mr / Ms + surname** (nama keluarga). Budi Santoso, kalau Santoso nama keluarganya → *Dear Mr Santoso,*, bukan *Dear Mr Budi* ✗: Mr + nama depan bukan kebiasaan bahasa Inggris, juga bukan kebiasaan Indonesia. Banyak orang Indonesia **hanya punya satu nama** (*Wahyudi*): itu nama lengkapnya, jadi *Dear Mr Wahyudi,* benar. Kalau kamu tidak yakin bagian mana nama keluarganya, tulis **nama lengkapnya**: *Dear Budi Santoso,*. Dengan rekan kerja Indonesia di Indonesia, *Dear Pak Budi,* / *Dear Bu Ani,* itu biasa dan sopan: itu kebiasaan lokal (Pak / Bu + nama panggilannya).

rows.id: Yth. Bapak Santoso,
rows.note: to Budi Santoso, if Santoso is his family name

id.note: untuk Budi Santoso, kalau Santoso nama keluarganya

rows.en: Dear Pak Budi,
rows.id: Yth. Pak Budi,
rows.note: to an Indonesian colleague in Indonesia

id.note: untuk rekan kerja Indonesia di Indonesia

rows.en: Dear Sir or Madam,
rows.id: Kepada Yth. Bapak/Ibu,

id.note: formal: kamu tidak tahu nama pembacanya

rows.en: Thank you for your help. Kind regards,
rows.id: Terima kasih atas bantuan Anda. Salam,
rows.note: a formal ending

rows.en: Thanks a lot, see you tomorrow!
rows.id: Makasih banyak, sampai ketemu besok!
rows.note: informal: a WhatsApp to a colleague

blocks.text:
**Indonesian habits to drop.**
1) *Hi Sir,* ✗. *Hi* is informal and *Sir* is very formal, so they don't mix. In writing, *Sir* without a name appears in *Dear Sir or Madam,*; *Sir* + a first name (*Sir Budi*) is a British title for a knight! Write *Dear Mr Lim,* or, locally, *Dear Pak Hasan,*. (Saying *Yes, sir* to a customer in a shop or a hotel is fine: the trap is in writing.)
2) *wanna* (= want to) and *gonna* (= going to) are spoken forms and chat spellings: never in an email. *Hi Sir, I wanna ask about the job* → *Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to enquire about the position.*
3) *Thanks a lot, see ya!* is for a friend. In a work email: *Thank you for your help. Kind regards,*.

id.text:
**Kebiasaan Indonesia yang perlu ditinggalkan.**
1) *Hi Sir,* ✗. *Hi* itu informal dan *Sir* sangat formal, jadi tidak bisa dicampur. Dalam tulisan, *Sir* tanpa nama muncul di *Dear Sir or Madam,*; *Sir* + nama depan (*Sir Budi*) adalah gelar ksatria di Inggris! Tulis *Dear Mr Lim,* atau, untuk lingkungan lokal, *Dear Pak Hasan,*. (Mengucapkan *Yes, sir* ke pelanggan di toko atau hotel tidak masalah: jebakannya ada di tulisan.)
2) *wanna* (= want to) dan *gonna* (= going to) adalah bentuk lisan dan ejaan chat: jangan dipakai di email. *Hi Sir, I wanna ask about the job* → *Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to enquire about the position.*
3) *Thanks a lot, see ya!* itu untuk teman. Di email kerja: *Thank you for your help. Kind regards,*.

blocks.prompt: You're writing an internal email in English to your manager, Budi Santoso, at your office in Jakarta. Everyone calls him Pak Budi. Which greeting is best?
blocks.explain: For an Indonesian colleague in Indonesia, **Dear Pak Budi,** is the normal, polite local custom. *Hi Sir* mixes informal *Hi* with very formal *Sir* and has no name, and *Sir* + a first name is a British knight's title. (*Dear Mr Santoso,* would also be correct, if Santoso is his family name.)

id.prompt: Kamu menulis email internal dalam bahasa Inggris untuk manajermu, Budi Santoso, di kantor di Jakarta. Semua orang memanggilnya Pak Budi. Salam mana yang paling tepat?
id.explain: Untuk rekan kerja Indonesia di Indonesia, **Dear Pak Budi,** adalah kebiasaan lokal yang biasa dan sopan. *Hi Sir* mencampur *Hi* yang informal dengan *Sir* yang sangat formal dan tidak ada namanya, dan *Sir* + nama depan adalah gelar ksatria di Inggris. (*Dear Mr Santoso,* juga benar, kalau Santoso nama keluarganya.)

What's the difference between enquire and inquire?
How do I write the greeting if an Indonesian name has no surname?
When should I use Yours sincerely?

id.intro: Di B1 kamu sudah belajar menulis email yang sopan. Sekarang kita lihat kata-kata di dalamnya: bahasa Inggris punya banyak pasangan seperti ask dan enquire, atau find out dan discover, yang artinya sama tapi tingkat formalitasnya berbeda. Kamu akan belajar padanan formal untuk kata sehari-hari dan phrasal verb, dan cara memilih yang tepat untuk lamaran kerja, klien, atau rekan kerja di WhatsApp.
suggestedQuestions: Apakah salah memakai phrasal verb di email formal?
Bagaimana menulis salam kalau nama orang Indonesia tidak punya nama keluarga?
Kapan aku sebaiknya pakai Yours sincerely?

assessment.fiv-1: Lengkapi balasan formal untuk klien ini dengan satu kata kerja formal yang berarti got (past simple, dalam bahasa Inggris): 'Dear Mr Lim, Thank you for your email. We ___ your payment of Rp 4,500,000 yesterday, and your order will arrive on Friday.'
assessment.fiv-2: Lengkapi pesan dari bank ini dengan satu kata formal (dalam bahasa Inggris) yang berarti enough: 'We are sorry, but there are not ___ funds in your account to complete this transfer.'
assessment.fiv-3: Lengkapi kalimat dari situs web hotel ini dengan satu kata kerja formal (dalam bahasa Inggris) yang berarti help: 'Our staff will be happy to ___ you with any questions about your booking.'
assessment.fiv-4: Buat kalimat dari laporan perusahaan ini lebih formal: ganti phrasal verb-nya dengan satu kata kerja dari bahasa Latin dalam bentuk yang sama. 'The IT department is looking into the problem with the payroll system.' Tulis kata kerja barunya saja.
assessment.fiv-5: Ganti went up dengan satu kata kerja formal dalam past simple, untuk laporan perusahaan: 'In 2025, the price of cooking oil in Surabaya went up by 15%.'
assessment.fiv-6: Kamu menulis email formal untuk seorang pembeli di perusahaan di Singapura. Namanya Andi Wijaya, dan Wijaya adalah nama keluarganya (surname). Tulis salam pembukanya dalam bahasa Inggris (boleh dengan atau tanpa koma).
assessment.fiv-7: Kamu mengirim pesan WhatsApp ke Dimas, rekan kerja yang duduk di dekatmu. Pesan mana yang lebih cocok untuk pembaca ini? Tulis A atau B. A: 'Could you inform me once the client arrives? Kind regards, Rina' B: 'Can you let me know when the client gets here? Thanks!'
